description: I'm a physics olympiad silver medalist and aspiring aerospace engineer passionate about astrophysics, artificial intelligence, and space exploration. I have experience in AI-based astronomy research, deep learning, and Unity flight simulation. I love combining physics and technology to solve real-world challenges.
summary:
What happens to a flame when gravity no longer pulls hot air upward? Fire behaves differently in space, and understanding why is important for keeping astronauts safe.

NASA has conducted experiments to study how flames behave in microgravity, but exploring the data and comparing results isn't always straightforward. That's why we created "SOLARIS".

SOLARIS is an interactive platform that brings NASA's combustion research into one place. Users can explore real BASS-II experimental records, compare test conditions, examine scientific findings, and identify questions that still need answers. We've also built "Cosmic Flame Lab", a 3D environment where users can explore how gravity and surrounding conditions might influence fire behavior through simplified physics-based simulations.

Throughout the project, we focused on one important principle: "real data and simulations should never be confused." SOLARIS makes that distinction clear, shows where the evidence is limited, and connects its findings to NASA's original research.

Our goal is to make microgravity combustion research easier to understand and more useful for students, researchers, and anyone interested in space science. We hope SOLARIS encourages further exploration and contributes, even in a small way, to making future spacecraft and space habitats safer.
details:
What We Built

We created SOLARIS because we noticed something: NASA has done a lot of valuable research on how fire behaves in space, but finding and understanding that information isn't always straightforward. Even when the experimental data is publicly available, comparing different tests and figuring out what the results actually tell us can be difficult.

We wanted to make that easier.

SOLARIS is an interactive research platform that brings together NASA's microgravity combustion research and gives people tools to explore it themselves. Rather than simply presenting information, we wanted users to be able to investigate the experiments, compare results, and ask their own questions.

How SOLARIS Works

The Data Atlas is one of the main parts of our platform. It contains 129 experimental records from NASA's Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) investigation. Users can search through these records, filter experiments, examine their conditions, and compare the available results.

We also built a research library covering 11 NASA investigations. It brings together information about what each investigation studied, how the experiments were conducted, and where users can find related publications.

One of the features we put particular effort into is Research Studio. While working with the data, we realized that comparing experiments isn't always as simple as it seems. Different experiments can use different materials, conditions, and measurements, which makes some comparisons more meaningful than others.

Research Studio helps users examine these differences, check whether experiments are suitable for comparison, identify missing information, and explore questions that future research might help answer.

We also created Cosmic Flame Lab, an interactive 3D environment where users can experiment with different gravitational and environmental conditions to see how they might influence flame behavior. It uses simplified physics-based models, so the results aren't intended to be exact predictions. The idea is to help people understand the underlying concepts through interaction rather than just reading about them.

Another part of SOLARIS is our Research Copilot, which uses Google Gemini to help users ask questions about NASA's combustion research and get explanations supported by relevant scientific sources.

What Makes SOLARIS Different

While developing SOLARIS, we didn't want to focus only on making the website look impressive. We wanted the scientific information behind it to be useful and presented responsibly.

One of the biggest things we learned was how careful you need to be when comparing scientific experiments.

Two experiments might seem similar at first, but differences in materials, oxygen levels, airflow, or other conditions can make their results difficult to compare directly. Simply putting two sets of numbers side by side doesn't necessarily tell the whole story.

We tried to address this by making it clear which information comes from actual NASA experiments, which comes from published research, and which comes from our own simplified simulations.

Our comparison tools are designed to help users notice important differences between experiments instead of assuming that every result can be compared directly.

We also wanted to be open about missing data and uncertainty. Sometimes the available evidence isn't enough to answer a question confidently, and we think it's important for users to recognize that.

For us, this became a central part of SOLARIS. Understanding the limits of the evidence matters just as much as understanding the results.

Technologies We Used

We used React and Vite to build the frontend and Three.js for the interactive 3D visualizations. Our backend was developed using Python and FastAPI, and we integrated the Google Gemini API to support the AI features in Research Copilot.

The scientific information in SOLARIS comes mainly from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and related NASA research publications.

We also used AI-assisted tools during development to help with programming, debugging, and research. However, a major part of our work was figuring out how to bring the different components together, organize the scientific information, and make the platform practical for people who want to explore the data.

Why It Matters and What's Next

Fire safety is already a serious concern on Earth, but in space, the problem becomes more complicated. Gravity affects how hot gases move, how flames spread, and how combustion develops. Understanding these differences is important as humans prepare for longer missions and possible habitats on the Moon and Mars.

We know SOLARIS can't replace actual laboratory experiments or professional spacecraft fire safety systems. That was never our intention.

What we want is to make the research that already exists easier to find, understand, and work with, especially for students and people who may not have much experience with combustion science.

There are still plenty of things we would like to improve. We'd like to add more experimental data, develop more accurate simulations based on validated scientific models, and create additional tools for investigating how fire behaves under different conditions.

We don't see SOLARIS as a finished solution to the challenges of space fire safety. We see it as a starting point that we can continue improving.

If it helps someone understand an experiment they previously found confusing, discover a gap in the available data, or come up with a new research question, then we've achieved something worthwhile.
